woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. Borderlands wears its ideological leanings openly from the first trailer. The female-dominated ensemble, the race-swapped Roland casting, and the girlboss Lilith protagonist were all visible in marketing materials long before release. Nothing is hidden or deployed as a late-film pivot. Conservative audiences who object to these choices had every opportunity to identify them before buying a ticket. This is a woke-leaning movie that advertised itself as such. Not a trap.

director.name: Eli Roth
director.ideology: MAINSTREAM HOLLYWOOD / APOLITICAL GENRE. Roth is known for ultra-violent horror (Hostel, The Green Inferno, Thanksgiving) and operates within the Hollywood studio system without a distinct ideological brand. His work tends toward exploitation and genre filmmaking rather than political messaging. The Green Inferno drew accusations of racism for its portrayal of indigenous cannibals, but Roth framed it as homage to Italian cannibal films. He also directed the 2018 Death Wish remake, a property associated with conservative self-defense themes. Roth's ideological footprint is inconsistent and commercially driven rather than activist.
director.profile: Eli Roth is an American filmmaker born April 18, 1972. He came to prominence with Cabin Fever (2002) and became a leading figure of the 'Splat Pack' with Hostel (2005) and Hostel: Part II (2007). His filmography includes The Green Inferno (2013), Knock Knock (2015), Death Wish (2018), The House with a Clock in Its Walls (2018), Thanksgiving (2023), and Borderlands (2024). Roth also appeared as an actor in Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds (2009). His directing career has bounced between horror, action, and family-friendly fare without a consistent ideological through-line. Borderlands represents his biggest-budget project and his biggest commercial failure. Reports indicate the studio was unhappy with Roth's original cut, leading to Tim Miller (Deadpool) being brought in for reshoots in early 2023. Craig Mazin, the original screenwriter and creator of HBO's Chernobyl and The Last of Us, removed his name from the project entirely, a devastating signal of creative disagreement. The final screenplay credit went to Roth and 'Joe Crombie,' with additional literary material credited to Aaron Berg, Oren Uziel, Juel Taylor, Tony Rettenmaier, Zak Olkewicz, Chris Bremner, and Sam Levinson. Seven additional writers on a single script is a reliable indicator of a troubled production.

writer.name: Eli Roth & Joe Crombie (screenplay); additional literary material by Aaron Berg, Oren Uziel, Juel Taylor, Tony Rettenmaier, Zak Olkewicz, Chris Bremner, Sam Levinson
writer.profile: The credited screenplay is by Roth and 'Joe Crombie.' Craig Mazin (Chernobyl, The Last of Us) originally wrote the screenplay but removed his name from the project in June 2023, declining even to use a pseudonym. 'Joe Crombie' has no other credits and is widely believed to be either a pseudonym for another writer or a composite credit. The WGA listed no hyperlink to a Joe Crombie member page. The additional literary material credits read like a casualty list: Aaron Berg wrote an initial R-rated draft in 2016. Oren Uziel rewrote in 2018. Juel Taylor and Tony Rettenmaier rewrote in 2021. Zak Olkewicz wrote new pages for Tim Miller's reshoots. Chris Bremner and Sam Levinson contributed additional material. Nine writers across eight years of development hell. The result reads exactly like what it is: a script written and rewritten by committee until every trace of personality was sanded off.

lead_producer.name: Ari Arad, Avi Arad, Erik Feig
lead_producer.company: Arad Productions / Picturestart / Gearbox Studios / 2K / Lionsgate

composer.name: Steve Jablonsky
composer.profile: Steve Jablonsky is an American composer best known for scoring the Transformers franchise (five films), as well as The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003), The Island (2005), Lone Survivor (2013), and Deepwater Horizon (2016). He is a protege of Hans Zimmer through Remote Control Productions. Jablonsky replaced Nathan Barr, who was originally attached to score Borderlands. His work on Borderlands is functional blockbuster scoring that serves the action sequences without being memorable or distinctive.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: Borderlands (2009), Borderlands 2 (2012), Borderlands 3 (2019) by Gearbox Software
fidelityCasting.assessment:
Borderlands has significant fidelity problems, though they're more about characterization than ideology in most cases.

Lilith: In the games, Lilith is a young, fiery Siren with supernatural powers. She's impulsive, dangerous, and physically youthful. Cate Blanchett was 54 during filming. The age gap changes the character fundamentally, turning a reckless young vault hunter into a world-weary bounty hunter with a tragic past. The movie also makes Lilith the undisputed protagonist when the games treat the vault hunters as an ensemble. The Firehawk revelation at the climax, while drawn from game lore, is deployed as a 'chosen one' moment that feels more like a Mary Sue coronation than anything in the source material.

Roland: The most controversial casting. In the games, Roland is a tall, muscular, serious ex-soldier. He's a stoic military leader who becomes commander of the Crimson Raiders in Borderlands 2. Kevin Hart is a 5'2" comedian known for manic energy and punchlines. The casting doesn't just change the character's physicality; it changes his entire personality. Hart's Roland is diminished to near-irrelevance in the film. Multiple viewers reported forgetting he was in the movie. The character is Black in the games, so this isn't a race swap. It's a personality, physicality, and gravitas swap. Hart trained with Navy SEALs to prepare, which says everything about the gap between what the role demanded and what he naturally brings.

Tiny Tina: Ariana Greenblatt is arguably the closest casting to the source material. Tina is young, chaotic, and explosive-obsessed in both the games and the film. The age and energy match.

Claptrap: Jack Black voices Claptrap, replacing the games' original voice actor David Eddings. Black's performance is adequate but lacks the grating, manic annoyingness that made Claptrap distinctive. The character is reduced to comic relief sidekick without the games' meta-humor.

Dr. Tannis: Jamie Lee Curtis plays Tannis as a quirky scientist. In the games, Tannis is deeply antisocial, possibly on the autism spectrum, and has a relationship with her ECHO recorder that borders on romantic. The film softens her considerably and recasts her as Lilith's foster mother, an invention with no basis in the source material.

Krieg: Florian Munteanu's Krieg looks the part physically but is reduced to a mostly silent bodyguard. In the games, Krieg is a psycho with a split personality and one of the most tragic backstories in the franchise. The film strips him down to muscle.

Overall Fidelity Score: LOW. The film borrows character names, basic visual design, and the concept of Pandora and the Vault from the games, but the characterizations, relationships, tone, and story are almost entirely original inventions that discard what made the source material beloved.

celebrityMentions.name: Cate Blanchett
celebrityMentions.context: Two-time Academy Award winner (Blue Jasmine, The Aviator) and one of the most respected actresses of her generation. Her involvement in Borderlands was puzzling to many industry observers. Blanchett herself attributed the decision partly to 'COVID madness' and her husband telling her the physical role 'could save her life.' Her performance was among the few elements that received any praise, though critics noted even she couldn't elevate the material. The role represents one of the most significant misfires in a career otherwise defined by prestige projects. At 54, Blanchett was roughly three decades older than the game's version of Lilith.

celebrityMentions.name: Kevin Hart
celebrityMentions.context: One of the highest-grossing comedians in Hollywood history. Hart's casting as Roland was the single most debated decision in the film's production. Roland in the games is a tall, stoic, muscular soldier. Hart is 5'2" and known exclusively for comedy. The casting was criticized not as a race swap (Roland is Black in the games) but as a fundamental misunderstanding of the character's identity. Hart trained with Navy SEALs to prepare for the role, which fans viewed as confirmation that the casting was wrong to begin with. His performance is reportedly so sidelined that audiences forgot he was in the film.

celebrityMentions.name: Jamie Lee Curtis
celebrityMentions.context: Academy Award winner for Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022). Curtis plays Dr. Patricia Tannis, reimagined as Lilith's foster mother. Like Blanchett, Curtis's involvement raised questions about what attracted A-list talent to such weak material. Her performance is competent but wasted on an underwritten role.

celebrityMentions.name: Jack Black
celebrityMentions.context: Voices Claptrap, the franchise's iconic robot sidekick. Black replaced David Eddings, who voiced Claptrap across the game series. Black's performance is serviceable but lacks the specific brand of annoying charm that made Claptrap a fan-favorite. The character's most notable scene involves it defecating, which Roth has said was inspired by watching his French bulldog poop.

celebrityMentions.name: Craig Mazin
celebrityMentions.context: Creator of HBO's Chernobyl and The Last of Us. Mazin wrote the original screenplay for Borderlands but removed his name entirely in June 2023, replaced by the mysterious 'Joe Crombie.' Mazin denied using a pseudonym and said he 'cannot claim any authorship' of the final film. This is the strongest signal possible that the screenplay was rewritten beyond recognition from his original vision. The contrast between Mazin's critically acclaimed The Last of Us adaptation and the Borderlands disaster illustrates how studio interference and development hell can destroy even strong source material.

celebrityMentions.name: Tim Miller
celebrityMentions.context: Director of Deadpool (2016) and Terminator: Dark Fate (2019). Miller was brought in to direct two weeks of reshoots in early 2023 after Roth became unavailable due to his commitment to Thanksgiving. Reports suggest the studio was unhappy with Roth's original cut, and Miller's involvement was more extensive than typical reshoots. The presence of a second director further fractured the film's already incoherent tonal identity.

celebrityMentions.name: Avi Arad
celebrityMentions.context: Israeli-American producer and former CEO of Marvel Entertainment. Arad produced dozens of early Marvel films including the Sam Raimi Spider-Man trilogy, X-Men, and Daredevil. His post-Marvel producing credits include Venom: Let There Be Carnage, Morbius, Madame Web, and Borderlands. The pattern of critically reviled, commercially underperforming adaptations has become a reliable predictor: if Avi Arad's name is on a video game or comic book movie in the 2020s, lower your expectations.

parentalGuidance.guidance: Borderlands is safely PG-13 and frankly could have been PG in terms of actual content. This is one of the film's biggest problems from a fan perspective: the Borderlands games are rated M for Mature with extreme violence, dark humor, and crude content. The movie strips all of that away. There is no blood, no gore, no sexual content, and no strong language. The action sequences are sanitized to the point of being toothless. Stunt coordinator Jimmy O'Dee confirmed that scenes depicting heads being blown up and limbs being severed were cut to maintain the PG-13 rating. For parents, the film is essentially harmless. Children 10 and up can watch it without concern. The real parental guidance note is about quality, not content: this is a very bad movie, and your kids' time would be better spent playing the actual games (which are rated M and should be evaluated separately).

summary.overall:
Borderlands is what happens when a studio spends $115 million trying to turn a beloved M-rated video game into a PG-13 Guardians of the Galaxy knockoff. The result is a film so creatively bankrupt that it debuted at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes, earned a D+ CinemaScore from opening-weekend audiences, grossed $33 million against a $115 million production budget (plus $30 million in marketing), and lost Lionsgate an estimated $80 million. It is, by every measurable standard, one of the worst major studio releases of 2024.

The premise borrows loosely from the games. Lilith (Cate Blanchett), a bounty hunter, is hired by Atlas (Edgar Ramirez), a corporate villain, to retrieve his kidnapped daughter Tiny Tina (Ariana Greenblatt) from the lawless planet Pandora. Once there, Lilith discovers that Atlas wants Tina for her ability to open an ancient alien vault. Lilith teams up with Roland (Kevin Hart), Krieg (Florian Munteanu), her foster mother Dr. Tannis (Jamie Lee Curtis), and the robot Claptrap (Jack Black) to protect Tina and reach the vault first.

If this sounds like every sci-fi action movie you've seen since 2014, that's because it is. The plot is a fetch quest interrupted by bus rides, convenient discoveries, and characters literally stumbling over plot devices. Lilith 'gets a feeling' about where to go. Things are found exactly when they need to be found. The vault key appears in an underground maze that the team navigates with minimal actual difficulty. Every narrative beat arrives on schedule with zero tension or surprise.

The ensemble, despite costing what must have been a significant portion of the budget in salary alone, generates approximately zero chemistry. Blanchett sleepwalks through a role that requires her to be a battle-hardened badass on a planet she abandoned as a child. She's a fine actress doing nothing with nothing. Hart's Roland is so marginal to the story that multiple reviewers reported forgetting he was in the film. The character who was a stoic military leader in the games becomes a background player who occasionally shoots things. Curtis collects a paycheck as the eccentric scientist foster mom. Jack Black voices Claptrap with the energy of someone recording dialogue during a lunch break.

The only cast member who seems calibrated to the material is Ariana Greenblatt as Tiny Tina, who brings actual manic energy to a role that demands it. Everyone else is either miscast, underwritten, or both.

The PG-13 rating is the film's original sin. Borderlands the video game franchise is defined by over-the-top violence, crude humor, dark comedy, and anarchic energy. The games are rated M for Mature. They feature exploding heads, rivers of blood, psychopaths screaming about meat, and humor that ranges from juvenile to genuinely transgressive. Stripping all of that away to chase a broader audience is like adapting Deadpool without the R rating. Oh wait, they did that too, and it also didn't work until they brought the R rating back.

Stunt coordinator Jimmy O'Dee confirmed that scenes with heads being blown up and feet being cut off were filmed and then cut to maintain PG-13. Eli Roth, a director whose entire career is built on graphic horror violence, was hired to make a sanitized family-friendly action comedy. The creative dissonance is staggering. Hiring Eli Roth and then telling him not to be Eli Roth is studio decision-making at its most self-defeating.

The production history tells the real story. Nine writers worked on the script across eight years. Craig Mazin wrote the original screenplay, then removed his name entirely. Tim Miller directed reshoots because Roth was busy with another movie. The studio reportedly hated Roth's original cut. The result is a film directed by two different people, written by nine different people, and produced by a committee that couldn't agree on what kind of movie they were making. It plays exactly like what it is: a corporate product assembled from spare parts by people who had conflicting visions and ultimately agreed on nothing.

The film's ideological content is secondary to its incompetence, but it's there. Lilith is structured as a Mary Sue. She has a tragic past, supernatural powers she doesn't know about, and the entire plot resolves when she accepts how special she truly is. The 'Firehawk' reveal at the climax is a chosen-one coronation that earns nothing because the film never builds toward it with any dramatic weight. The female-dominated ensemble relegates every male character to villain (Atlas), sidekick (Claptrap, Roland), or near-mute muscle (Krieg). This isn't an inherently woke choice. Plenty of great films center women. But when the male characters are systematically stripped of competence, agency, and screen time to ensure the female lead shines, it starts to look less like storytelling and more like quota-filling.

Kevin Hart's Roland is the most glaring example. In the games, Roland is the leader. He's a commanding military presence. He dies heroically in Borderlands 2 in a moment that devastated the fan community. In the movie, he's a short comedian doing a 'serious' turn that the film doesn't know how to use, so it mostly doesn't. Hart trained with Navy SEALs to prepare for a role that the script forgot to write.

The box office tells the definitive story. $8.6 million opening weekend. $33 million total worldwide. Against a combined production and marketing budget north of $145 million. Lionsgate lost an estimated $80 million. The film was pulled to digital just three weeks after theatrical release, an unprecedented speed that tells you exactly how fast the studio wanted to stop the bleeding.

Borderlands joins a long list of video game adaptations that failed because the people making them didn't understand or didn't care about what made the source material work. The Borderlands games are anarchic, violent, funny, and self-aware. The movie is sterile, safe, unfunny, and oblivious. It took everything distinctive about the franchise, sanded it down to nothing, and served the remainder in a Guardians of the Galaxy costume that doesn't fit.

10% on Rotten Tomatoes. 48% audience score. D+ CinemaScore. $80 million in losses. A stacked cast of Oscar winners and box office draws couldn't save it. Borderlands isn't just a bad video game movie. It's a case study in how not to adapt anything.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative viewers will find Borderlands mildly annoying on the ideological front but mostly just boring. The girlboss structure is present but not aggressive enough to be genuinely offensive. It's more lazy than ideological. The real problem is quality. The film is tedious, unoriginal, and wastes its entire cast. If you're looking for ideological ammunition, there's some here: the female-first ensemble that sidelines every male character, the Mary Sue protagonist, the casting choices that prioritize star power and demographic boxes over character accuracy. But honestly? The movie isn't interesting enough to generate real outrage. It's not trying to lecture you. It's trying to be a fun space adventure and failing at every level. Save your money. Play the games instead. They're actually good, actually funny, and actually R-rated.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for sequences of action and violence, some suggestive material, and language. Despite the M-rated source material, the film contains no blood, no gore, no strong language, and no sexual content. The action is thoroughly sanitized. A robot defecates on screen for comedy. Some dark underground environments may be mildly scary for very young children. Safe for ages 10 and up. The bigger concern is your children's taste in cinema. This is bad enough to potentially damage their developing appreciation for good filmmaking.

tropeAudit.name: Girlboss Protagonist / Mary Sue
tropeAudit.description: Lilith is the textbook Mary Sue. She has a tragic backstory (abandoned Pandora as a child), hard-as-nails competence in every situation, and supernatural powers she discovers at the climax. The entire plot exists to reveal how special she truly is. She is the 'Firehawk,' an Eridian who can open the Vault. Every other character orbits her journey of self-acceptance. The film never challenges her, never lets her fail in a meaningful way, and never gives her a flaw that actually costs her anything. She 'gets feelings' that conveniently point her toward plot objectives. She survives a grenade blast that should have killed her. She single-handedly resolves the climax by accepting her destiny. In the games, Lilith is one of four playable characters in an ensemble. In the movie, she's the center of the universe. The authenticity multiplier is 1.0 (moderate) rather than 1.4 (low) because Lilith IS a powerful Siren in the source material. The Mary Sue treatment is amplified by the film, but the character's power set has some basis in the games.

tropeAudit.name: Systematic Male Marginalization
tropeAudit.description: Every significant male character in Borderlands is either a villain (Atlas), comic relief (Claptrap), a near-mute brute (Krieg), or a sidelined afterthought (Roland). The three characters with actual agency, narrative arcs, and emotional weight are all female: Lilith, Tiny Tina, and Tannis. This is not inherently woke in isolation. Many great films center women. But the systematic stripping of male competence and screen time, combined with the elevation of every female character, creates a pattern that goes beyond natural storytelling. Kevin Hart's Roland, who leads the Crimson Raiders in the games, is reduced to a background player whose most notable contribution is occasionally shooting things. The authenticity multiplier is 1.4 (low) because the Borderlands games feature a balanced ensemble where male characters like Roland, Brick, and Mordecai are just as central as female characters. The film's gender hierarchy is an invention, not a faithful adaptation.

tropeAudit.name: Source Material Character Alteration (Roland)
tropeAudit.description: Roland's casting is not a race swap (the character is Black in the games). It's something arguably worse from a fidelity perspective: a complete personality, physicality, and gravitas swap. Game Roland is tall, muscular, stoic, and a natural leader. Movie Roland is Kevin Hart: 5'2", manic, comedic, and functionally irrelevant to the plot. This feels less like a creative reinterpretation and more like casting a famous name regardless of fit. The decision to cast a comedian in a soldier role, then give him almost nothing to do, suggests the priority was attaching a bankable name rather than honoring the character. Scored as woke because the net effect is the diminishment of the most prominent male hero from the games.

tropeAudit.name: Sanitization of Source Material
tropeAudit.description: The Borderlands games are rated M for Mature. They feature extreme gore, crude sexual humor, dark comedy about mental illness and violence, and a tone that revels in transgression. The film strips every bit of edge away. No blood. No gore. No strong language. No crude humor beyond a robot pooping. The PG-13 rating transforms a franchise built on anarchic excess into a sanitized family-friendly product. Stunt coordinator Jimmy O'Dee confirmed that filmed scenes with exploding heads and severed limbs were cut. This sanitization isn't directly ideological, but the impulse to file down every rough edge to maximize commercial appeal maps onto the same risk-averse, offense-avoiding instinct that drives much of modern progressive content curation. The game's irreverent, boundary-pushing humor was its identity. Removing it is removing the soul.

tropeAudit.name: Corporate Villain as Sole Male Authority
tropeAudit.description: Atlas, the film's primary antagonist, is the only male character with actual power and authority. He's a ruthless corporate magnate who exploits his own daughter and threatens to kill a child. Every other male character is subordinate, marginalized, or serves as comic relief. The villain-as-only-powerful-man trope reinforces the film's implicit message that male authority is inherently corrupt while female solidarity is inherently redemptive. Minor trope because Atlas is also a villain in the games, though the games distribute villainy and heroism across genders more evenly.

tropeAudit.name: Found Family / Chosen Bonds
tropeAudit.description: The film's central emotional arc is about forming a surrogate family. Lilith reconciles with her foster mother Tannis. She becomes a protective figure for Tiny Tina. The ragtag group of strangers bonds into a unit that chooses each other over self-interest. This is a genuinely traditional value: the idea that loyalty, sacrifice, and chosen bonds matter more than blood ties or institutional allegiance. The execution is terrible, but the thematic intention is sound.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Protection and Sacrifice
tropeAudit.description: Lilith's arc culminates in protecting Tiny Tina from Atlas's exploitation. The Tannis-Lilith foster mother relationship, while invented for the film, reinforces traditional maternal values. Tannis raised Lilith when she was abandoned. Lilith pays it forward by protecting Tina. The film presents maternal instinct and intergenerational female care as its highest moral value. This is traditional in structure even if the execution is weak.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Corporate / Individual vs. Institution
tropeAudit.description: Atlas represents unchecked corporate power that treats people, including his own daughter, as tools. The heroes' rejection of Atlas's authority and their triumph over his private army carries a populist, anti-institutional message that resonates with conservative skepticism of corporate overreach. However, this is extremely generic and functions more as standard blockbuster villainy than genuine ideological commentary.

tropeAudit.name: Self-Reliance and Competence
tropeAudit.description: The protagonists survive by their own wits, combat skills, and resourcefulness rather than institutional support. They are outlaws and misfits who don't rely on government, law enforcement, or authority structures. This rugged individualism is a traditional value, though the film undercuts it by making Lilith's success depend on her inherent genetic destiny (being an Eridian) rather than earned skill.

tropeAudit.name: Rejection of Authoritarian Control
tropeAudit.description: The heroes explicitly reject Atlas's attempt to control Tina and exploit the Vault's technology. They destroy his communication device, fight his private army, and ultimately trap him inside the Vault. The message that no one person or corporation should control powerful technology resonates faintly with libertarian and conservative principles, but the execution is too shallow to register as genuine thematic commentary.

This is a modernized musical remake that wears its progressive updates on its sleeve from the first frame.

director.name: Samantha Jayne & Arturo Perez Jr.
director.ideology: MODERATE PROGRESSIVE. Jayne and Perez Jr. are a married couple whose prior work consists of Hulu's Quarter Life Poetry series. They were first-time feature directors selected by Tina Fey and Lorne Michaels. Their creative choices lean progressive (social media integration, diversity casting, explicit queer representation) but they are functionally executing Fey's vision rather than imposing their own ideological framework.
director.profile: Samantha Jayne and Arturo Perez Jr. are a wife-and-husband directing team based in Los Angeles. Their primary prior credit is Quarter Life Poetry, a short-form series for Hulu based on Jayne's Instagram poetry account of the same name. Mean Girls (2024) was their feature film directorial debut. They were hired in September 2021 by Paramount Players. Their approach to the material emphasized visual energy, social media aesthetics, and phone-screen cinematography to bring the story into the smartphone era. Neither director has a significant public ideological profile beyond the creative choices visible in the film itself. They deferred extensively to Fey as screenwriter and producer.

writer.name: Tina Fey
writer.profile: Tina Fey wrote the screenplay, adapted from her own book for the Broadway musical, which was itself adapted from her original 2004 screenplay, which was based on Rosalind Wiseman's nonfiction book Queen Bees and Wannabes. Fey is one of the most prominent comedy writers in American entertainment, best known for 30 Rock (2006-2013) and her tenure as head writer and Weekend Update anchor on Saturday Night Live. She is openly progressive-leaning, with a comedic style that historically skewered both left and right but has increasingly tilted toward mainstream liberal sensibilities. Her decision to sanitize much of the original film's edgier humor for the 2024 version, remove the Coach Carr statutory rape subplot, excise racial slurs and terms like 'retarded,' and make Janis explicitly queer rather than ambiguously so, all reflect a conscious modernization toward contemporary progressive norms. Fey also served as producer and reprised her role as Ms. Norbury.

lead_producer.name: Lorne Michaels, Tina Fey
lead_producer.company: Broadway Video / Little Stranger / Paramount Pictures

composer.name: Jeff Richmond
composer.profile: Jeff Richmond is Tina Fey's husband and longtime musical collaborator. He composed the music for the Mean Girls Broadway musical (lyrics by Nell Benjamin) and returned to adapt and compose the score for the film version. His prior credits include composing the score for 30 Rock, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, and various SNL segments. Richmond also served as executive producer on the film. His musical sensibility is pop-Broadway, accessible and upbeat without being particularly distinctive.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: Mean Girls (2004 film) / Mean Girls (Broadway musical, 2018)
fidelityCasting.assessment: The 2024 film is adapted from the Broadway musical, which itself was adapted from the 2004 film. Three of the six main student roles have been race-swapped from the original cast. Janis Ian, played by white actress Lizzy Caplan in 2004, is now Janis 'Imi'ike, played by Native Hawaiian actress Auli'i Cravalho. Damian Hubbard, played by white actor Daniel Franzese, is now played by Black actor Jaquel Spivey. Karen Smith, played by white actress Amanda Seyfried, is now Karen Shetty, played by Indian-American actress Avantika Vandanapu. The characters' surnames were changed to reflect their new ethnic backgrounds. Gretchen Wieners (Bebe Wood) now references Latinx heritage through a mention of her 'abuelo.' Cady Heron (Angourie Rice) and Regina George (Reneé Rapp) remain white, preserving the two most iconic roles from the original. Aaron Samuels (Christopher Briney) also remains white. Reneé Rapp previously played Regina George on Broadway as a replacement cast member, making her the only principal actor to carry a role from the stage version to the film. The most significant character change beyond race is Janis, who was ambiguously rumored to be a lesbian in the 2004 film (it was used as a slur by Regina), but is now explicitly and openly queer. This change was promoted as a deliberate update by the filmmakers. The removal of Cady's father from the story (he existed in the 2004 film) is another notable deviation, making Ms. Heron a single mother without explanation.

celebrityMentions.name: Tina Fey
celebrityMentions.context: Writer, producer, and co-star. Fey has been the creative architect of every version of Mean Girls across two decades: the 2004 film, the Broadway musical, and this 2024 adaptation. Her decision to sanitize the humor, diversify the cast, and make Janis explicitly queer represents a conscious alignment with contemporary progressive entertainment norms. She reprises her role as Ms. Norbury.

celebrityMentions.name: Reneé Rapp
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Regina George. Rapp is the breakout star of the film, having previously played the role on Broadway. She is an openly queer pop artist whose debut album Snow Angel (2023) explored her bisexuality. Her public persona and fanbase skew progressive and LGBTQ+. Her performance is widely regarded as the film's strongest element.

celebrityMentions.name: Auli'i Cravalho
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Janis 'Imi'ike. Cravalho is best known as the voice of Moana in Disney's 2016 animated film. She came out as bisexual on TikTok in 2020. Her casting as Janis, who is now explicitly queer in the story, dovetails with her own public identity. She has been vocal about the importance of representation in media.

celebrityMentions.name: Lindsay Lohan
celebrityMentions.context: Original Cady Heron in the 2004 film. Makes a cameo appearance as the moderator of the Mathletes tournament, a nostalgic callback for fans of the original. Fey chose Lohan as the sole original cast cameo because 'the original movie is really Lindsay's movie.'

celebrityMentions.name: Megan Thee Stallion
celebrityMentions.context: Appears as herself in social media montage sequences. Also performed the end credits song with Reneé Rapp. Her inclusion signals the film's intention to court Gen Z and social media culture.

celebrityMentions.name: Jazz Jennings
celebrityMentions.context: Makes a brief cameo as a 'Social Media Friend' in the same montage sequences. Jennings is a transgender activist and reality TV personality known for the TLC series I Am Jazz. This is a blink-and-miss inclusion, but it's worth knowing about for conservative audiences tracking representation in mainstream entertainment.

celebrityMentions.name: Lorne Michaels
celebrityMentions.context: Producer. The legendary Saturday Night Live creator produced both the 2004 original and this 2024 version through Broadway Video. His involvement ensures institutional continuity with the original film's production lineage.

parentalGuidance.guidance: Rated PG-13 for sexual material, strong language, and teen drinking. Recommended for viewers 13 and older. This is significantly tamer than the 2004 original in terms of raw edginess. The statutory rape subplot involving Coach Carr has been completely removed. Racial slurs and the word 'retarded' have been excised. However, the film has added explicit LGBTQ+ content that was only implied in the original, including an openly queer Janis and a same-sex kiss played casually in the background. The Halloween sequence features provocative costumes and sexual humor involving characters who are supposed to be 16-17 years old, which parents should be aware of. The musical format and bright visual style make this feel lighter and more family-friendly than the original, but the themes of social cruelty, manipulation, and betrayal remain intact. Conservative parents should know that the diversity recasting, explicit queerness, and occasional progressive asides (references to fracking, redlining) are present but not overwhelming. This is a teen comedy musical, not ideological cinema.

tropeAudit.name: Diversity Recasting of Established Characters
tropeAudit.description: Three of six main student roles were race-swapped from the 2004 original. Janis Ian becomes Janis 'Imi'ike (Native Hawaiian via Auli'i Cravalho), Damian becomes Black (Jaquel Spivey), and Karen Smith becomes Karen Shetty (Indian-American via Avantika). Character surnames were changed to match. Gretchen Wieners gains Latinx heritage. The Broadway musical had already diversified, so this is less of a cold swap and more of an ongoing evolution across versions. Still, the 2004 film is the primary cultural reference point for audiences, and these changes are among the most visible and discussed aspects of the remake. Authenticity scores moderate because the story is set in a diverse suburban high school, making mixed-race casting plausible, but the deliberate name changes signal ideological intent rather than colorblind casting.

tropeAudit.name: Explicit LGBTQ+ Representation (Janis)
tropeAudit.description: In the 2004 original, Janis was rumored to be a lesbian as a slur spread by Regina. Whether she actually was queer was left ambiguous. The 2024 film makes Janis explicitly and proudly queer. Her queerness is treated as known and accepted by her friends. The actress, Auli'i Cravalho, is herself openly bisexual and was cast with this character choice in mind. Janis's sexuality now functions as a key element of her identity and her backstory with Regina, not merely as a rumor weaponized against her. This shifts the character from 'victim of homophobic gossip' to 'out and proud,' which is a meaningful ideological reframing. Centrality is high because Janis is one of the three main characters.

tropeAudit.name: Sanitized Humor / Self-Censorship
tropeAudit.description: The 2024 film systematically removes edgy humor from the 2004 original. The Coach Carr statutory rape subplot is gone entirely. The word 'retarded' is removed. 'Dyke' is removed. The clique description scene no longer shows racial groupings. The 'is your muffin buttered' sexual innuendo setup is removed but its punchline is kept, making the joke land awkwardly. Multiple critics and audiences noted that the humor feels 'toothless' and 'sanitized' compared to the original, which made fun of everyone equally. This self-censorship is an authenticity score of 1.0 because it is clearly deliberate and reflects the filmmakers' own choices about what modern audiences should and shouldn't laugh at.

tropeAudit.name: Casual Same-Sex Affection (Background)
tropeAudit.description: During the clique introduction sequence, two male students are shown kissing. This is played casually as background detail, normalized without comment. It is a brief moment but noticeable. In a high school setting, this is plausible and not forced, but its inclusion is a deliberate choice to signal LGBTQ+ normalization.

tropeAudit.name: Single Mother Without Explanation
tropeAudit.description: In the 2004 film, Cady's parents were a married couple who had been living in Africa for her father's work. In the 2024 version, Cady's mother (Jenna Fischer) is a single parent. Her father is never mentioned, referenced, or explained. The change is silent and total. While single-parent households are common and realistic, the deliberate removal of an existing father from a remake, without any narrative justification, reads as an ideological choice to center a strong independent mother figure.

tropeAudit.name: Progressive Political Asides
tropeAudit.description: Two random lines reference fracking and redlining, injected into dialogue with no setup or narrative justification. These feel like Tina Fey's personal politics briefly seizing the microphone. They are throwaway moments that don't affect the plot, but they signal the filmmakers' political alignment. Low centrality, but the lack of organic connection to the story pushes authenticity toward the 'injected' end.

tropeAudit.name: Trans/LGBTQ+ Activist Cameo
tropeAudit.description: Jazz Jennings, a transgender activist and reality TV personality, makes a brief cameo as a 'Social Media Friend' in a montage sequence. This is a blink-and-miss moment. Most viewers won't recognize Jennings. But her inclusion is a deliberate signal of trans solidarity in a mainstream teen film. Similarly, Megan Thee Stallion appears as herself, though her inclusion is more about Gen Z cultural relevance than ideology.

tropeAudit.name: Girl Power / Female Solidarity Messaging
tropeAudit.description: The film's climactic moral is that girls need to stop tearing each other down and start supporting each other. Ms. Norbury's gym intervention, Cady's Spring Fling speech, and an elaborate musical number all drive this home. The 'be yourself' and 'women should support women' messaging is the film's thesis statement. This was present in the 2004 original too, but the 2024 version leans into it harder with less comedic counterbalance. The original's version had more ironic distance; this one plays it straight with full musical production values.

tropeAudit.name: Sexualized Minors for Comedy
tropeAudit.description: The Halloween sequence features the teenaged characters in provocative costumes with an entire musical number about how Halloween is an excuse for girls to dress 'sexy.' The song simultaneously critiques and participates in the sexualization. The actresses are adults playing teenagers, but the characters are explicitly 16-17. This was present in the 2004 original as well, but the 2024 version gives it a full musical number treatment, amplifying the screen time. This trope straddles woke and traditional lines but scores as woke because of its framing as feminist commentary on double standards rather than simple titillation.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences for Bad Behavior
tropeAudit.description: The film's core arc is a morality tale. Cady is corrupted by popularity, becomes cruel, and faces real consequences: she loses her friends, gets suspended from school, and must earn her way back through genuine effort (joining the Mathletes and winning the competition). Regina George's cruelty catches up with her both socially and physically (hit by a bus, played for dark comedy). The Burn Book's exposure forces a school-wide reckoning. Every character who behaves badly faces consequences. The film treats moral choices as serious, even within its comedic framework.

tropeAudit.name: Redemption Through Personal Responsibility
tropeAudit.description: When the Burn Book is exposed, Cady takes full responsibility for her actions rather than deflecting blame. She accepts her suspension, joins the Mathletes to earn extra credit, and personally apologizes to everyone she hurt, including Regina. Her redemption is earned through accountability and effort, not through being let off the hook. This is a straightforwardly traditional moral framework: you did wrong, you own it, you make it right.

tropeAudit.name: Academic Achievement Rewarded
tropeAudit.description: Cady's mathematical talent is established early and becomes the vehicle for her redemption. She deliberately fails math to get closer to Aaron, which is presented as a mistake and a betrayal of her own abilities. Aaron himself calls her out for dumbing herself down. Her eventual return to the Mathletes and her performance at the state championship represents a restoration of authentic self-respect through intellectual honesty. The message that pretending to be dumb to attract a boy is wrong is a genuinely positive lesson.

tropeAudit.name: Authenticity Over Social Status
tropeAudit.description: The film's resolution involves Cady choosing genuine friendships (Janis and Damian) over social climbing (the Plastics). Her Spring Fling Queen speech, in which she breaks the crown and distributes pieces to other girls, is a rejection of hierarchical social status in favor of inclusive community. While the execution is saccharine, the underlying message that popularity is hollow and real relationships require vulnerability and honesty is a perennially conservative social value.

tropeAudit.name: Teacher as Moral Authority
tropeAudit.description: Ms. Norbury (Tina Fey) functions as the film's moral compass. Her gym intervention, where she forces the junior girls to confront their behavior, is presented as wise, necessary, and effective. She is not undermined, mocked, or proven wrong. Mr. Duvall (Tim Meadows) is played more for comic relief but still represents institutional authority that ultimately supports the right outcome. Traditional respect for teachers as moral guides is preserved.

summary.overall:
Here's the thing about Mean Girls (2024): it's not the culture war flashpoint that either side wants it to be.

The film is a musical adaptation of a Broadway musical that was itself adapted from a 2004 movie that was based on a nonfiction parenting book. It has been filtered through so many layers of adaptation that the result is less a bold creative statement and more like a photocopy of a photocopy, with some TikTok filters slapped on top.

The plot is identical to the original. Cady Heron (Angourie Rice), a homeschooled kid raised in Kenya, enrolls at a suburban high school and gets pulled into the orbit of the Plastics: Regina George (Reneé Rapp), Gretchen Wieners (Bebe Wood), and Karen Shetty (Avantika). Her real friends, Janis (Auli'i Cravalho) and Damian (Jaquel Spivey), convince her to infiltrate the Plastics and take Regina down from the inside. Cady becomes the thing she set out to destroy. She loses her friends, gets suspended, takes responsibility, joins the Mathletes, wins the state championship, gets crowned Spring Fling Queen, breaks the crown, and gives a speech about how everyone is special.

You know this story. Your mom knows this story. The question is whether this particular retelling justifies its existence.

The answer is: barely. And it's mostly because of Reneé Rapp.

Rapp, who played Regina on Broadway, is the single best reason to watch this film. She brings a volcanic confidence and comedic precision that elevates every scene she's in. Her musical numbers are the film's highlights by a wide margin. When Rapp is on screen, the movie crackles. When she's not, it flatlines into pleasant mediocrity. Angourie Rice is a perfectly competent Cady but lacks the scrappy charm Lindsay Lohan brought to the role. Christopher Briney's Aaron Samuels is forgettable. Bebe Wood's Gretchen is solid. Tim Meadows phones it in as Mr. Duvall, a real disappointment given how funny he was in the original.

The musical numbers range from genuinely fun (Regina's villain songs, the Halloween sequence) to generic and unmemorable. Jeff Richmond's compositions are pop-Broadway competent but not distinctive. You'll tap your feet during the film and forget every melody by the time you reach your car. The spoken dialogue scenes between musical numbers often feel like connective tissue rather than storytelling.

Now, the ideological scorecard.

The most discussed changes from the original are the diversity recasting and the explicit queering of Janis. Three of six main student roles were race-swapped: Janis is now Native Hawaiian, Damian is Black, and Karen is Indian-American. Character surnames were changed accordingly. Janis, who was rumored to be a lesbian in the 2004 film (used as a slur by Regina), is now openly and proudly queer. These are the changes that sparked the 'is Mean Girls 2024 woke?' search traffic.

Here's an honest assessment: the diversity casting is real, deliberate, and ideologically motivated. Changing character names to match new ethnicities signals that this isn't colorblind casting. It's deliberate ethnic rebranding. But does it hurt the movie? Not really. Jaquel Spivey's Damian is arguably an improvement over the original. Avantika's Karen is fun. Cravalho's Janis is strong. The performances work on their own terms.

The more meaningful change is the humor. The 2004 Mean Girls worked because it was ruthlessly equal-opportunity in its satire. It made fun of everyone: popular girls, nerds, teachers, parents, every racial group, every social class. Nobody was safe. The 2024 version has filed down nearly every sharp edge. The Coach Carr statutory rape subplot is gone. The word 'retarded' is gone. 'Dyke' is gone. The racial clique descriptions are sanitized. Jokes that once had bite now arrive pre-chewed.

This is the real cost, and it's not small. The original's genius was that it treated teenagers as smart enough to handle uncomfortable humor. The remake treats them as too fragile for it. The result is a film that is pleasant, safe, and forgettable where the original was sharp, risky, and quotable for two decades running.

There are a few random progressive asides that feel like Tina Fey editorializing: a throwaway line about fracking, another about redlining. Neither has any connection to the plot. They're there, they're noticeable, and they're annoying in the way that any gratuitous political aside is annoying in a teen comedy.

Jazz Jennings makes a blink-and-miss cameo as a 'Social Media Friend.' Megan Thee Stallion appears as herself in social media montages. These are demographic targeting choices more than ideological statements.

But here's what the culture war reading misses: underneath the progressive packaging, the film's moral engine is surprisingly traditional. Cady's corruption by popularity is treated as a genuine moral failing. She doesn't get let off the hook. She gets suspended, loses her friends, and has to earn her way back through effort and accountability. The film takes personal responsibility seriously. Bad behavior has consequences. Redemption requires work, not just feelings.

The message about dumbing yourself down for a boy is explicitly rejected. Aaron calls Cady out for pretending to fail math, and the film treats this as a turning point. Academic achievement is presented as valuable and authentic. The Mathletes victory is played as genuinely triumphant.

Ms. Norbury functions as a credible moral authority. The gym intervention scene, where she forces the girls to confront their cruelty, is played straight and presented as wise. Teachers as moral guides is a deeply traditional concept, and the film respects it.

The social media framing is the film's most genuinely contemporary element. The 2004 version dealt with hallway gossip and physical Burn Books. The 2024 version deals with viral humiliation, Instagram stories, and the permanent digital footprint of cruelty. This update is earned and effective. The horror of online bullying resonates differently than hallway gossip, and the film handles it with reasonable intelligence.

So what do we have? A musical remake that race-swaps half the cast, makes a queer subtext into queer text, removes most of the original's comedic edge, throws in a couple of political asides nobody asked for, but also delivers a morality tale about personal responsibility, academic integrity, and the consequences of cruelty. It's woke-leaning, not woke-drenched. The progressive elements are real but they don't overwhelm the film's fundamentally traditional moral framework.

It made $105 million worldwide on a $36 million budget. It holds a 71% on Rotten Tomatoes. It's a modest commercial success and a critical shrug. It's not the disaster conservatives feared or the triumph progressives wanted. It's a perfectly average musical remake of a comedy classic, carried by one exceptional performance and hampered by the decision to sand down everything that made the original stick.

The original Mean Girls was lightning in a bottle. This one is lightning in a Tupperware container. Same basic ingredients, none of the spark.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults approaching this film should calibrate expectations accordingly. This is not a progressive polemic. It's a teen musical comedy that leans left in its casting and character choices but tells a fundamentally traditional story about consequences, accountability, and the hollowness of social status. The diversity recasting is visible and intentional. Janis being openly queer is explicit. A couple of political asides about fracking and redlining are gratuitous but brief. Jazz Jennings appears for about two seconds. None of this dominates the viewing experience. The film's actual moral message, that bad behavior has consequences, that pretending to be dumb for boys is wrong, that personal responsibility matters, is one conservatives can endorse. The real frustration for adult viewers won't be ideology. It'll be mediocrity. If you love the 2004 original, this version will feel like a watered-down cover song of a classic track. The musical numbers are fine but forgettable. The humor is safe to the point of blandness. Reneé Rapp as Regina George is worth watching. The rest is take-it-or-leave-it. Watch with your teenagers if you want. You won't be offended. You probably won't be entertained enough to remember it a week later, either.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The film's feminist and empowerment themes are front and center from the opening act. The source material is one of the most widely discussed BookTok novels in history, with its domestic violence subject matter being the primary reason for its fame. Marketing materials, trailers, and press coverage all make the film's thematic territory obvious. There is no delayed ideological pivot. The traditional elements, particularly the maternal protection arc and the moral seriousness of the intergenerational abuse cycle, are equally present throughout.

director.name: Justin Baldoni
director.ideology: MODERATE/FAITH-BASED. Baldoni is a practicing Baha'i whose previous directorial work includes faith-adjacent tearjerkers like Five Feet Apart (2019) and Clouds (2020). His worldview leans toward spiritual universalism, service to others, and emotional sincerity rather than partisan ideology.
director.profile: Justin Baldoni first became known as Rafael Solano on Jane the Virgin (2014-2019). His directorial career has focused on emotionally earnest dramas, often centered on illness or loss. Five Feet Apart (2019) was a cystic fibrosis romance. Clouds (2020) was a Disney+ biographical drama about a teenager with cancer. Both films were sincere, conventional, and commercially viable without being politically charged. Baldoni is an outspoken member of the Baha'i faith, which emphasizes the unity of humanity, gender equality, and service. He has given TED talks about redefining masculinity, though from a spiritual rather than progressive-activist framework. His approach to It Ends with Us was reportedly more grounded and serious than what the final theatrical cut reflects, as Lively's editorial influence shifted the tone toward a glossier, more romanticized aesthetic. The behind-the-scenes conflict between Baldoni and Lively became a bigger cultural event than the film itself, resulting in dueling lawsuits and a PR war that became a proxy battle for broader culture-war grievances about feminism, MeToo, and celebrity accountability.

writer.name: Christy Hall
writer.profile: Hall is a screenwriter and producer whose prior credit is Daddio (2023), a chamber-piece drama starring Sean Penn and Dakota Johnson set entirely inside a taxi. She also served as a producer on It Ends with Us. Hall adapted Colleen Hoover's novel with a focus on the emotional interiority of Lily Bloom, and her script reportedly served as the foundation that both Baldoni's original cut and Lively's preferred edit worked from. Ryan Reynolds also contributed uncredited dialogue to a rooftop scene, allegedly written before the WGA strike. Hall's sensibility leans toward intimate character drama rather than overt ideology.

lead_producer.name: Alex Saks, Jamey Heath, Blake Lively, Christy Hall

composer.name: Rob Simonsen & Duncan Blickenstaff
composer.profile: Simonsen has scored films including The Spectacular Now (2013), The Age of Adaline (2015), and Love, Simon (2018). His work tends toward lush, emotionally accessible romantic drama scoring. Blickenstaff contributed additional music. The score for It Ends with Us is functional and emotionally supportive without being distinctive.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: It Ends with Us by Colleen Hoover (2016)
fidelityCasting.assessment: The adaptation is largely faithful to the novel's plot structure and key emotional beats. The most significant deviation is tonal: the novel treats Lily's internal conflict with raw, often uncomfortable honesty about her attraction to Ryle even as the abuse escalates, while the film, particularly in Lively's preferred editorial cut, glamorizes Lily's world with lush production design, aspirational fashion, and a romantic sheen that some critics argued undercut the gravity of the domestic violence. The rooftop meet-cute, which Ryan Reynolds reportedly rewrote, is more comedic and banter-heavy than the novel's version. The ending remains faithful: Lily asks Ryle for a divorce, invoking their daughter's future safety, and Ryle agrees. The novel's epilogue with Atlas is preserved. The casting of Blake Lively as Lily was divisive among book fans, who pictured someone less glamorous and more relatable. Brandon Sklenar's Atlas was generally well-received. Baldoni's Ryle was considered effective, though the off-screen drama between actor and co-star made it impossible to evaluate the performance without cultural baggage.

celebrityMentions.name: Blake Lively
celebrityMentions.context: Lead actress and producer. Became the center of a massive cultural backlash for her tone-deaf promotional tour, during which she pushed her haircare line and encouraged moviegoers to wear floral outfits rather than engaging with the film's domestic violence themes. Later filed a sexual harassment lawsuit against Baldoni. Her public persona became a culture-war flashpoint about celebrity privilege, feminism, and accountability.

celebrityMentions.name: Justin Baldoni
celebrityMentions.context: Director and co-star who plays the abuser Ryle Kincaid. After Lively's promotional backlash, Baldoni's more measured approach to discussing domestic violence earned him public sympathy. He subsequently sued Lively, Ryan Reynolds, and their publicist for civil extortion and defamation. The case remains ongoing as of early 2026.

celebrityMentions.name: Ryan Reynolds
celebrityMentions.context: Lively's husband. Contributed uncredited dialogue to the film's rooftop scene. Named as a defendant in Baldoni's countersuit. His involvement in the film's editing and promotional strategy reportedly exacerbated tensions with Baldoni.

celebrityMentions.name: Colleen Hoover
celebrityMentions.context: Author of the source novel, which became a BookTok phenomenon. Hoover served as executive producer. She publicly sided with Lively during the promotional controversy, though her own work has faced criticism for allegedly romanticizing toxic relationships across her bibliography.

celebrityMentions.name: Taylor Swift
celebrityMentions.context: Lively's close friend. Was present at the film's premiere and posted support on social media. Her association with the film was seen by some critics as emblematic of the celebrity ecosystem that insulated Lively from genuine engagement with the domestic violence subject matter.

parentalGuidance.guidance: Despite the PG-13 rating, this film deals with extremely heavy subject matter. The domestic violence scenes are not graphic in a horror-movie sense, but they are emotionally brutal and realistic enough to disturb younger viewers and potentially trigger survivors of abuse. The attempted rape scene, while not explicit, is deeply unsettling. Parents should be aware that the film's glossy, romantic aesthetic may lull younger viewers into thinking this is a standard romance before the abuse escalates. The film provides no content warning before screening. Recommended for mature teens 15+ who can process the material in context, ideally with a parent available for discussion afterward.

summary.overall:
It Ends with Us arrives as two films at war with each other, and the battle behind the camera turned out to be far more interesting than what ended up on screen.

The story is straightforward. Lily Bloom (Blake Lively) is a florist in Boston who falls for Ryle Kincaid (Justin Baldoni), a charismatic neurosurgeon. Their romance accelerates quickly. Then Ryle hits her. Then he apologizes. Then it happens again. Meanwhile, Lily's first love, Atlas Corrigan (Brandon Sklenar), reappears in her life, offering a reminder of what love looks like without violence. Flashbacks reveal that Lily's father abused her mother throughout her childhood. The question the film poses is whether Lily will repeat her mother's pattern or break it.

She breaks it. And here is where the film's ideological scorecard gets interesting.

The feminist reading is obvious and the marketing leaned into it: Lily's decision to leave Ryle is framed as empowerment, self-actualization, a woman refusing to accept the narrative that love requires suffering. The title itself is a declaration of agency. The divorce is presented as liberation. The flower shop is financial independence made literal. The reunion with Atlas is the reward for choosing yourself.

But underneath the empowerment gloss, the film's actual moral engine runs on deeply traditional fuel. Lily does not leave Ryle because she discovers her authentic self or because a therapist tells her she deserves better. She leaves because she has a daughter. The moment that breaks the cycle is not feminist consciousness-raising. It is maternal instinct. Lily looks at baby Emerson and sees the future: either her daughter grows up watching her mother get hit, or she doesn't. The decisive scene, where Lily asks Ryle to imagine their daughter being abused by a future partner, is an appeal to parental responsibility, not feminist theory. It is a profoundly conservative argument dressed in progressive clothing.

The film also takes marriage seriously, which is not something empowerment narratives typically do. Lily does not leave Ryle casually. She agonizes. She gives him chances. She hopes therapy will work. The divorce is not gleeful or triumphant. It is treated as a necessary and painful last resort, which is exactly how traditional moral frameworks understand the dissolution of marriage: permissible when all other options are exhausted, especially when children are at risk.

The intergenerational cycle is the film's most powerful theme and its most conservative one. Lily's mother stayed with an abusive husband. Lily nearly does the same thing. The film argues that personal choices echo across generations, that children inherit their parents' failures unless someone has the courage to absorb the cost of change. This is not systemic analysis. This is personal moral responsibility, which is the bedrock of conservative ethical thought.

But the film undercuts its own seriousness in ways that are hard to ignore. Blake Lively's Lily is aspirational to the point of fantasy. She runs a gorgeous flower shop that apparently generates enough revenue to support a Boston lifestyle. Her wardrobe is immaculate. Her apartment looks like a Pinterest board. The domestic violence scenes feel like interruptions in a lifestyle commercial rather than the central reality of the character's life. This is partly a directorial choice (or an editorial one, given the behind-the-scenes conflict), and partly a star-power problem: Lively brings such effortless glamour to the role that the ugliness of abuse never fully penetrates the surface.

Baldoni's performance as Ryle is the film's most underrated element. He plays the abuser not as a monster but as a damaged man who genuinely loves Lily and genuinely cannot control his rage. The film's refusal to offer Ryle a redemption arc is brave. The revelation that his childhood trauma (accidentally killing his brother) fuels his violence does not excuse it, and crucially, the film knows this. Allysa's warning to Lily, that she should not take Ryle back despite his trauma, is the most morally clear-eyed moment in the script.

Brandon Sklenar's Atlas is warm and appealing but underwritten. He exists primarily as a contrast to Ryle: proof that male tenderness is possible, that Lily's first instinct about love was correct. Jenny Slate provides welcome comic relief as Allysa but is also saddled with the film's most emotionally complex secondary role, and she handles both registers well.

The controversy surrounding the film dwarfed the film itself. Lively's promotional tour, in which she sold haircare products, encouraged floral dress codes, and treated the press junket like a party rather than a conversation about domestic violence, became a defining cultural moment of 2024. Baldoni's more somber approach to discussing the material earned him public sympathy, which then shifted when Lively filed her sexual harassment complaint, which then shifted again when Baldoni filed his countersuit. The whole spectacle became a Rorschach test: feminists saw a woman being smeared for speaking up, conservatives saw celebrity entitlement weaponizing victimhood. Neither reading is entirely wrong.

As a piece of filmmaking, It Ends with Us is competent but unexceptional. The direction is workmanlike. The pacing drags in the second act. The flashback structure creates emotional distance rather than deepening it. The score is forgettable. The cinematography is pretty in a way that works against the material.

But the core story, stripped of the celebrity drama and the marketing mishaps, lands. A woman looks at her daughter, looks at her mother's life, and decides that the cycle stops here. That decision is dressed in the language of empowerment, but its roots are in sacrifice, maternal duty, and the belief that your choices matter across generations. It is, despite everything, a film that believes in personal responsibility more than systemic critique. That is worth noting.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find more to appreciate here than they might expect from a BookTok romance adaptation starring Blake Lively. The film's central argument is that a mother's primary obligation is to protect her children, even at enormous personal cost. The divorce is not celebrated as liberation; it is presented as the only moral option when all alternatives have been exhausted. The intergenerational abuse cycle is treated as a matter of personal moral courage, not systemic analysis. The film never blames society, institutions, or patriarchy for Ryle's violence. It blames Ryle. And it shows Lily taking responsibility for her own future rather than waiting for someone else to rescue her. The girlboss entrepreneur elements are present but relatively muted. The real engine is maternal love and the willingness to sacrifice comfort for your child's safety. Where the film may frustrate conservative viewers is in its glossy, aspirational tone, which sometimes trivializes the seriousness of its own subject matter, and in its refusal to engage with the possibility of reconciliation or redemption for the abuser.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for domestic violence, sexual content, and some strong language. Recommended for viewers 15 and older. Multiple scenes depict domestic violence including slapping, shoving, being pushed down stairs, and an attempted sexual assault. Childhood flashbacks show a father beating a mother. Several implied sex scenes with partial nudity. The film's glossy romantic aesthetic may make it attractive to younger teens who are not prepared for the abuse content. No content warning is provided at the start of the film. Parents should preview this before allowing younger teens to watch, and should be prepared for a conversation about domestic violence, healthy relationships, and the cycle of abuse.

tropeAudit.name: Female Empowerment as Central Narrative Arc
tropeAudit.description: Lily's journey is framed as a feminist empowerment arc: from victim to survivor, from passive acceptance to active choice. The title itself declares agency. The flower shop is financial independence. The divorce is self-determination. The reunion with Atlas is the reward for choosing yourself. This framing is the film's primary language, even if the underlying moral logic is more traditional than the packaging suggests.

tropeAudit.name: Divorce Presented as Liberation
tropeAudit.description: The film frames Lily's divorce from Ryle as a heroic act. The final scenes treat the dissolution of the marriage as a moral victory. While the circumstances (ongoing domestic violence, protecting a newborn) provide legitimate justification within any moral framework, the film's tone treats divorce as empowerment rather than as a painful necessity. The distinction matters for how audiences internalize the message.

tropeAudit.name: Male Abuser Without Redemption Arc
tropeAudit.description: Ryle is presented as irredeemable despite his genuine love for Lily and his childhood trauma. The film provides context for his violence (accidentally killing his brother as a child) but explicitly argues through Allysa's character that this context does not justify reconciliation. While this is a morally defensible position, the complete refusal to engage with the possibility of genuine change or redemption leans into a modern framework where abusers are permanently categorized rather than potentially redeemable.

tropeAudit.name: Female Independence Over Marriage
tropeAudit.description: The film's epilogue shows Lily thriving as a single mother with a successful business. Her meeting with Atlas at the farmers' market suggests romantic possibility but on her terms. The message is that a woman's wholeness does not depend on being in a relationship. This is a mild but consistent undercurrent throughout the film.

tropeAudit.name: Girlboss Entrepreneur Fantasy
tropeAudit.description: Lily opens a thriving flower shop that seems implausibly successful and beautiful for a first-time business owner. The entrepreneurial success functions as a visual metaphor for female capability and independence but also as lifestyle-porn wish fulfillment that undercuts the film's grittier themes.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Protection as Moral Imperative
tropeAudit.description: The decisive moment of the entire film is not a feminist awakening but a maternal one. Lily leaves Ryle because she has a daughter. The scene where she asks Ryle to imagine Emerson being abused by a future partner is the moral fulcrum. The film argues that a mother's highest duty is protecting her child from harm, even at the cost of her marriage, her comfort, and her hopes for the relationship. This is the oldest and most deeply conservative of all parenting arguments.

tropeAudit.name: Intergenerational Moral Responsibility
tropeAudit.description: The film's central metaphor is the cycle of abuse passing from one generation to the next. Lily's father beat her mother. Lily nearly repeats her mother's choice to stay. The film argues that individual moral courage is required to break destructive family patterns. This is personal responsibility framed across time, not systemic critique. Your parents' sins become yours unless you actively choose differently.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences of Choices Treated with Gravity
tropeAudit.description: Every choice in the film carries weight. Ryle's childhood accident warps his entire adult life. Lily's decision to give Ryle multiple chances costs her physically and emotionally. Her mother's decision to stay shaped Lily's entire psychology. The film takes the moral weight of personal decisions seriously in a way that aligns with traditional ethical thinking: choices matter, they compound, and they shape the people around you.

tropeAudit.name: Marriage Treated with Moral Seriousness
tropeAudit.description: The film does not treat Lily's marriage casually. She does not leave at the first sign of trouble. She agonizes, hopes for change, gives second chances. The divorce is presented as a last resort after every alternative has been exhausted. This is closer to a traditional understanding of marital obligation than a modern disposability framework. The marriage matters, which is why leaving it is treated as sacrifice rather than convenience.

tropeAudit.name: Sacrificial Motherhood / Mother-Daughter Bond
tropeAudit.description: The film's emotional spine runs through three generations of mothers and daughters. Jenny stayed with Andrew and Lily suffered for it. Lily refuses to repeat that choice for Emerson's sake. The epilogue shows Lily, her mother Jenny, and baby Emerson visiting Andrew's grave together, three generations connected by the weight of the cycle that was finally broken. The mother-daughter bond is presented as the mechanism through which both trauma and healing are transmitted.
